question: How long must an authorised representative keep the technical paperwork for a general-purpose AI?
answer: The authorised representative must keep the technical documentation for **10 years after the general-purpose AI model has been placed on the market** [Art. 54(3)].

question: Under Article 8(2), if my product includes a high-risk AI system and is covered by other EU product laws, can I combine the required paperwork and testing?
answer:
Yes. Where your product contains a high-risk AI system and is also covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, you "shall have a choice of integrating, as appropriate, the necessary testing and reporting processes, information and documentation" into the documentation and procedures already required under those other laws, in order to "ensure consistency, avoid duplication and minimise additional burdens" [Art. 8(2)].

This is not legal advice.
judge_reason: Accurate and well-cited answer to Art. 8(2), but omits the caveat that the provider remains fully responsible for compliance with all applicable harmonisation legislation, and does not mention related single-documentation provisions in the retrieved excerpts.

question: Can a high-risk AI be sold or used before its conformity checks are finished?
answer: No. A high-risk AI system cannot be placed on the market or put into service before the conformity assessment is completed: the provider must “ensure that the high-risk AI system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure … prior to its being placed on the market or put into service” [Art. 16]. Importers must likewise verify, before placing the system on the market, that “the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 has been carried out by the provider” [Art. 23(1)], and both the provider and the system must be registered in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service [Art. 49(1)].
judge_reason: The answer says a flat 'No' and omits the Art. 46(1) derogation that lets a market surveillance authority authorise temporary placing on the market or putting into service for exceptional reasons; it also overstates Art. 49(1) registration (Annex III only, with a carve-out) and the retrieved excerpts did not include Art. 46.

question: How long do EU countries or the Commission have to object to a temporary measure taken against a risky AI system before it is considered justified?
answer: Three months, reduced to 30 days for non-compliance with the prohibitions in Article 5. [Art. 79(8)]
judge_reason: Answer is correct and well grounded; it omits that the period runs from receipt of the Art. 79(5) notification and the measure is a provisional one by another Member State's authority.

question: Under Article 60(4)(h), what do providers need to do when they team up with deployers for real-world testing?
answer: When providers or prospective providers organize real-world testing in cooperation with one or more deployers or prospective deployers, they must: inform those deployers of all aspects of the testing relevant to their decision to participate, and give them the relevant instructions for use of the AI system referred to in Article 13; and conclude an agreement with the deployer or prospective deployer specifying their roles and responsibilities to ensure compliance with the testing provisions under the Regulation and other applicable Union and national law [Art. 60(4)(h)].

question: Before asking a general-purpose AI provider to take action, can the AI Office talk to them first?
answer: Yes. Before a measure is requested, the AI Office may initiate a structured dialogue with the provider of the general-purpose AI model [Art. 93(2)]. The same option exists before sending a request for information [Art. 91(2)] and prior to requesting access to the model, to gather information on internal testing, safeguards and mitigation procedures [Art. 92(7)]. If, during the Article 93 dialogue, the provider of a model with systemic risk offers commitments to implement mitigation measures, the Commission may make those commitments binding and declare no further grounds for action [Art. 93(3)].

question: When I register a high-risk AI tool, do I need to include user instructions and a link for more info?
answer: Yes. When registering a high-risk AI system, you must submit the **electronic instructions for use**, except for high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7 [Annex VIII, Section A, points 12–13]. A **URL for additional information is optional**, not mandatory [Annex VIII, Section A, points 12–13].

question: If my company already has a monitoring plan under other EU laws, can we just add the AI Act requirements to it instead of making a new one?
answer: Yes, but only in the specific cases covered: for high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, providers “shall have a choice of integrating” the required elements into systems and plans already existing under that legislation, provided this achieves “an equivalent level of protection” [Art. 72(4)]. The same applies to Annex III point 5 high-risk AI systems placed on the market by financial institutions subject to Union financial-services-law internal governance requirements [Art. 72(4)]. The AI Act still requires the monitoring system/plan to meet the general requirements, including being proportionate and documented [Art. 72(1)] and based on a plan forming part of the technical documentation [Art. 72(3)]. This is not legal advice.
judge_reason: Accurate and well-grounded; minor omission that the Art. 72(3) template should be used and that integration is limited to post-market monitoring (the 'monitoring plan' interpretation is stated implicitly).

question: Under Article 93(3), what can the Commission do if a general-purpose AI provider promises to fix a systemic risk during talks?
answer: The Commission may, by decision, make those commitments binding and declare that there are no further grounds for action [Art. 93(3)].

question: What authorities does each EU country have to set up to enforce the AI Act?
answer:
Each EU Member State must set up or designate the following authorities:

*   **Notifying authorities**: At least one per Member State, responsible for assessment, designation, notification and monitoring of conformity assessment bodies [Art. 28(1)]. Member States must communicate their identity to the Commission [Art. 70(2)].
*   **Market surveillance authorities**: Member States must designate these and communicate their identity and tasks to the Commission; one market surveillance authority must be designated as the **single point of contact** for the Regulation [Art. 70(2)].
*   **National competent authorities**: Member States must ensure these are provided with adequate technical, financial, human resources and infrastructure [Art. 70(3)].
*   **Public authorities or bodies protecting fundamental rights**: By 2 November 2024, each Member State must identify these, make a list publicly available, and notify it to the Commission and other Member States [Art. 77(2)].
*   **AI regulatory sandboxes**: Member States must ensure their competent authorities establish at least one sandbox at national level (operational by 2 August 2026) [Art. 57(1)].
judge_reason: Omits the Art. 70(1) core rule (at least one notifying and one market surveillance authority as national competent authorities, acting independently and impartially) and misstates the national competent authorities bullet as a separate authority; the public-authorities bullet cites Art. 77(2) without clarifying what the paragraph 1 bodies are.

question: Who else can get involved in AI regulatory sandboxes to help businesses and governments cooperate?
answer:
Other relevant actors within the AI ecosystem can get involved to facilitate cooperation with the public and private sectors. These include notified bodies, standardisation organisations, SMEs (including start-ups), enterprises, innovators, testing and experimentation facilities, research and experimentation labs, European Digital Innovation Hubs, centres of excellence, and individual researchers [Art. 58(2)(f)].

Additionally, national competent authorities may allow for the involvement of other actors within the AI ecosystem and cooperate with other relevant authorities [Art. 57(4)], and where personal data is processed, national data protection authorities and other national or competent authorities are associated with the sandbox’s operation [Art. 57(10)].

question: Can EU countries ask the scientific panel's experts for help with enforcing the AI rules?
answer: Yes. Member States may call upon experts of the scientific panel to support their enforcement activities under this Regulation [Art. 69(1)].

question: Can the EU ask general-purpose AI model makers for information if scientists need it for their work?
answer: Yes, under specific conditions. Upon a duly substantiated request from the scientific panel, the Commission may issue a request for information to a provider of a general-purpose AI model, where the access to information is necessary and proportionate for the fulfilment of the tasks of the scientific panel under Article 68(2) [Art. 91(3)]. The provider (or its representative, or authorized persons/lawyers) shall supply the information requested [Art. 91(5)]. Note that later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.
judge_reason: Accurate and well-cited answer; the closing note about later amendments is a minor unneeded addition, and 'authorized persons/lawyers' paraphrase of Art. 91(5) slightly compresses the responsibility point.

question: Can providers of high-risk AI systems check their own compliance without using an external organization?
answer:
Yes. For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers must use the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control, which “does not provide for the involvement of a notified body” [Art. 43(2)]. For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, the provider may opt for internal control under Annex VI, unless specific exceptions apply (such as the absence of harmonised standards or their partial application) [Art. 43(1)].

The internal control procedure requires the provider itself to verify quality management system compliance, examine the technical documentation, and check that the design, development and post-market monitoring are consistent with that documentation [Annex VI]. This reflects the general rule that conformity assessment for high-risk AI systems (other than those related to products) is carried out by the provider under its own responsibility [Recital 125].
judge_reason: Minor gap: does not mention that high-risk AI systems under Annex I Section A product legislation (Art. 43(3)) follow the product-law conformity procedure, which may involve a notified body.

question: Who appoints the official EU bodies that help with AI testing?
answer: The Commission appoints them. [Art. 84(1)]

question: Can the Commission bring in outside experts to help evaluate general-purpose AI models?
answer: Yes. The Commission may appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations of general-purpose AI models on its behalf, including experts from the scientific panel established under Article 68 [Art. 92(2)]. These independent experts must meet the criteria set out in Article 68(2): particular expertise and competence in AI, independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models, and an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively [Art. 68(2)]. The Commission is to adopt implementing acts setting out the detailed arrangements and conditions for such evaluations, including the arrangements for involving and selecting independent experts [Art. 92(6)].

question: Can the rules for what goes into technical documentation be updated as technology changes?
answer: Yes. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend Annex IV (which sets out the required content of technical documentation) "in light of technical progress" to ensure the documentation provides all necessary information for compliance assessment [Art. 11(3)].

question: What does the Commission have to do when a new European technical standard is officially published?
answer: When a reference to a harmonised standard is published in the Official Journal of the European Union, the Commission shall repeal the implementing acts (common specifications) adopted under Article 41(1), or the parts thereof, that cover the same requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III or, as applicable, the same obligations set out in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter V [Art. 41(4)].
judge_reason: Accurate and well-cited answer to the publication step, but it omits the preceding obligation to assess the standard under Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 when it is proposed for publication.

question: Do I need to register my high-risk AI system in an EU database before I start selling or using it?
answer: Yes. Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (except point 2 of Annex III), the provider or authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database [Art. 49(1)]. Before putting into service or using such a system, deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies (or persons acting on their behalf) must also register themselves, select the system and register its use [Art. 49(3)], and they must comply with these registration obligations and shall not use the system if it is not registered [Art. 26(8)]. Additionally, if a provider concludes that an Annex III system is not high-risk under Article 6(3), they must still register themselves and that system before placing it on the market or putting it into service [Art. 49(2)].

question: Can using personal data in an AI regulatory sandbox affect the people whose data is being used or their privacy rights?
answer:
Under the conditions set out in Article 59(1), using personal data in an AI regulatory sandbox must **not** affect the data subjects or their privacy rights: any processing in the sandbox must "neither lead to measures or decisions affecting the data subjects nor ... affect the application of their rights laid down in Union law on the protection of personal data" [Art. 59(1)(f)].

However, the same provision requires that there are "effective monitoring mechanisms to identify if any high risks to the rights and freedoms of the data subjects ... may arise during the sandbox experimentation, as well as response mechanisms to promptly mitigate those risks and, where necessary, stop the processing" [Art. 59(1)(c)]. The data must also be held in a "functionally separate, isolated and protected data processing environment" with access limited to authorised persons [Art. 59(1)(d)], must be protected by "appropriate technical and organisational measures" and deleted when participation ends or the retention period expires [Art. 59(1)(g)], and processing logs must be kept for the duration of participation [Art. 59(1)(h)].

question: Do the confidentiality rules in Article 78(4) prevent authorities from sharing warnings or giving information in criminal cases?
answer: No. Article 78(4) expressly preserves those rights and obligations: paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 "shall not affect the rights or obligations of the Commission, Member States and their relevant authorities, as well as those of notified bodies, with regard to the exchange of information and the dissemination of warnings, including in the context of cross-border cooperation," nor "the obligations of the parties concerned to provide information under criminal law of the Member States" [Art. 78(4)].

question: When is an AI system considered to present a risk?
answer: An AI system is considered to present a risk when it presents risks to the health or safety, or to fundamental rights, of persons — in that case it is understood as a “product presenting a risk” under Article 3, point 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 [Art. 79(1)].

question: Who can cancel a delegation of power, and does it affect rules that are already in place?
answer: The European Parliament or the Council may revoke the delegation of power at any time [Art. 97(3)]. Such a revocation shall not affect the validity of any delegated acts already in force [Art. 97(3)].
judge_reason: No issues; minor omission of when revocation takes effect, but the question's two parts are fully answered.

question: Which EU border, travel, and migration databases are listed in the AI Act?
answer:
The AI Act lists the following EU border, travel, and migration databases and systems in Annex X:

*   **Eurodac** [Annex X, points 3–5]
*   **Entry/Exit System (EES)** [Annex X, points 3–5]
*   **European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS)** [Annex X, points 3–5]

Annex X also lists the **European Criminal Records Information System on third-country nationals and stateless persons (ECRIS-TCN)** and the **Interoperability** framework as large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice [Annex X, points 6–7].
citations: Annex X, points 3–5; Annex X, points 6–7
judge_reason: The answer correctly lists Eurodac, EES, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN and Interoperability from Annex X, but omits that points 1-2 (e.g. SIS/VIS) exist in Annex X, and the 'large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice' label is not in the excerpts.

question: Why do high-risk AI tools need to be tested?
answer:
High-risk AI systems must be tested to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures, to ensure they perform consistently for their intended purpose and comply with the requirements of the Regulation, and to confirm their expected performance before they are placed on the market or put into service [Art. 9(6)] [Art. 3(32)].

Testing must be performed at any time during development and, in any event, prior to placing the system on the market or putting it into service, against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate to the intended purpose [Art. 9(8)]. It also forms part of the provider’s quality management system, which must include examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development [Art. 17(1)(d)]. Additionally, training and testing on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting of intended use creates a presumption of conformity with certain data requirements [Art. 42(1)]. Testing may also include real-world conditions [Art. 9(7)] [Art. 60(2)].
judge_reason: Minor: the 'compliance with the requirements of the Regulation' wording slightly broadens Art. 9(6) ('requirements set out in this Section'), and the answer adds peripheral detail beyond the core purpose.

question: What kind of things do notified bodies have to report to the notifying authority?
answer:
Under the provided provisions, notified bodies must make available and submit, upon request, **all relevant documentation, including the providers’ documentation**, to the notifying authority [Art. 34(3)]. This is to allow that authority to conduct its assessment, designation, notification and monitoring activities [Art. 34(3)].

The other excerpts do not address additional reporting duties of notified bodies to the notifying authority; they instead cover the notifying authority’s own obligations to inform the Commission and other Member States of notifications and changes [Art. 30(2), Art. 36(1)], and the steps the notifying authority must take following restriction, suspension or withdrawal of a designation [Art. 36(7)].
judge_reason: The answer misses the actual reporting duties of Art. 45(1) (certificates issued, refusals/suspensions/withdrawals, circumstances affecting notification scope, requests from market surveillance authorities, activities on request) and wrongly implies the only duty is documentation submission on request.

question: When do EU countries have to tell the European Commission about their penalty rules?
answer: Member States must notify the Commission of their rules on penalties and other enforcement measures "without delay and at the latest by the date of entry into application," and must notify any subsequent amendments "without delay" [Art. 99(2)]. Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.
judge_reason: The answer is correct and matches Art. 99(2); the only blemish is an unsupported closing sentence about amendments to the Act, which is not backed by the excerpts.

question: What language do AI conformity certificates need to be written in?
answer: According to the EU AI Act, certificates issued by notified bodies must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established [Art. 44(1)].

question: Can the European Commission ask for access to an AI model's source code or APIs?
answer:
Yes. Under the AI Act, the European Commission may request access to a general-purpose AI model through APIs or other appropriate technical means, including source code, for the purpose of conducting evaluations [Art. 92(3)]. Such a request must state the legal basis, purpose and reasons, set the period for access to be provided, and mention the fines for failure to provide access [Art. 92(4)], and the provider (or its authorized representative) must supply the requested access [Art. 92(5)]. Prior to making the request, the AI Office may first initiate a structured dialogue with the provider to gather information on internal testing, safeguards and risk-mitigation measures [Art. 92(7)]. Separately, the Commission may also request documentation and additional information from providers of general-purpose AI models to assess compliance [Art. 91(1)], including, upon a substantiated request from the scientific panel, where necessary and proportionate for the panel's tasks [Art. 91(3)].

Note that access to source code for high-risk AI systems is governed by different provisions addressed to market surveillance authorities, not the Commission [Art. 74(13)].
judge_reason: Accurate and well-cited; the only minor issues are the loose 'for the purpose of conducting evaluations' phrasing (Art. 92(1) not in excerpts) and a slightly awkward closing clause on Art. 91(3).

question: What information must an AI provider include in their application for a quality management system check?
Who leads the EU AI Board and organises its meetings?
answer: The Board is chaired by one of the representatives of the Member States [Art. 65(8)]. The AI Office provides the secretariat, convenes the meetings upon request of the Chair, and prepares the agenda [Art. 65(8)].

question: What happens if an AI provider fails to prove its general-purpose model does not pose systemic risks?
answer: If a provider fails to demonstrate that its general-purpose AI model does not present systemic risks, the Commission shall reject those arguments, and the model **shall be considered to be a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk** [Art. 52(3)]. Consequently, the provider must then comply with the additional obligations applicable to such models, including performing model evaluation with adversarial testing, assessing and mitigating systemic risks at Union level, reporting serious incidents, and ensuring adequate cybersecurity protection [Art. 55(1)].

question: Who can ask the EU's AI testing centers for technical or scientific advice?
answer: According to the provided provisions, Union AI testing support structures shall provide independent technical or scientific advice at the request of **the Board, the Commission, or market surveillance authorities** [Art. 84(2)].

question: If a provider already has to report incidents under other EU laws, what do they need to report for high-risk AI?
answer: If a provider is already subject to equivalent reporting obligations under other Union legislative instruments, or if the high-risk AI system is a safety component of (or is itself) a device covered by Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and (EU) 2017/746, the notification of serious incidents is **limited to those referred to in Article 3, point (49)(c)** [Art. 73(9)] [Art. 73(10)].
judge_reason: The answer blends Art. 73(9) and 73(10) without noting that (9) applies only to Annex III systems, that (10) adds notification to a nationally chosen authority, and without saying what Art. 3(49)(c) covers.

question: How long do other EU countries or the Commission have to object to an AI authorisation before it is automatically accepted?
answer: Other EU countries or the Commission have **15 calendar days** from receipt of the notification/information to object; if no objection is raised, the authorisation is **deemed justified** [Art. 46(4)]. The objection period is counted from receipt of the information referred to in paragraph 3 [Art. 46(3)], and objections within those 15 calendar days trigger Commission review [Art. 46(5)].

question: What is the maximum fine for an EU institution that uses banned AI practices?
answer: The maximum administrative fine is **EUR 1 500 000** [Art. 100(2)]. This applies to non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 (the banned practices) by Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies [Art. 100(2)], where such prohibited practices include, for example, emotion inference in workplace and education institutions [Art. 5(1)(f)] or untargeted scraping of facial images [Art. 5(1)(e)].

question: What does the EU Commission do after a country takes action against a risky AI system?
answer:
After a Member State takes action against a risky AI system, the Commission evaluates the national measure and decides whether it is justified.

Under the Union safeguard procedure, where the Commission considers the national measure justified, all Member States must take appropriate restrictive measures such as requiring withdrawal of the AI system from their market; where the Commission considers it unjustified, the Member State concerned must withdraw the measure [Art. 81(2)].

For compliant AI systems that present a risk, the Commission must without undue delay consult the Member States concerned and relevant operators, evaluate the national measures taken, decide whether the measure is justified, and where necessary propose other appropriate measures [Art. 82(4)].
judge_reason: Accurate and well-cited, but the opening 'after a Member State takes action' is not tied to a specific scenario and mixes the Art. 81 (non-compliant systems) and Art. 82 (compliant but risky systems) procedures, with the Art. 81 consultation/evaluation step not shown in the excerpts; minor framing gaps only.

question: Before asking to see a general-purpose AI, what can the AI Office do to learn about its safety?
answer:
Before requesting access to the model itself, the AI Office may initiate a **structured dialogue** with the provider to gather information on the model’s safety measures. Specifically, prior to requesting access, it may gather more information on “internal testing of the model, internal safeguards for preventing systemic risks, and other internal procedures and measures the provider has taken to mitigate such risks” [Art. 92(7)].

The AI Office may also initiate a structured dialogue before sending a request for documentation or information [Art. 91(2)] and before requesting measures [Art. 93(2)].

question: What details must be included in an access request under Article 92(4)?
What do market surveillance authorities have to report every year under Article 74(2)?
answer:
Under Article 74(2), market surveillance authorities must make two annual reports:

*   To the Commission and relevant national competition authorities: any information identified in the course of market surveillance activities that may be of potential interest for the application of Union law on competition rules [Art. 74(2)].
*   To the Commission: the use of prohibited practices that occurred during that year and the measures taken [Art. 74(2)].

question: Can the same person who evaluates an AI testing body also decide on its official notification?
answer: No. Under the EU AI Act, the same person cannot both assess a conformity assessment body and decide on its notification. Notifying authorities must be organised so that “decisions relating to the notification of conformity assessment bodies are taken by competent persons different from those who carried out the assessment of those bodies” [Art. 28(4)].

question: What needs to be included in the technical paperwork for an AI system regarding its conformity and how it is checked after release?
answer:
The technical documentation must be drawn up before the AI system is placed on the market or put into service, kept up to date, and drawn up to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2, containing at a minimum the elements set out in Annex IV [Art. 11(1)].

**Conformity**
It must include a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 [Annex IV, points 8–9]. For conformity assessment, the provider must lodge an application including the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV with a notified body, which shall examine it and may require further evidence, tests, or access to training data and models [Annex VII, point 4].

**Post-market monitoring**
It must include a detailed description of the system in place to evaluate the AI system performance in the post-market phase, including the post-market monitoring plan referred to in Article 72(3) [Annex IV, points 8–9]. The post-market monitoring plan shall be part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV [Art. 72(3)]. It must also contain detailed information about the monitoring, functioning and control of the AI system, in particular regarding: capabilities and limitations in performance and degrees of accuracy; foreseeable unintended outcomes and sources of risks; human oversight measures; and specifications on input data [Annex IV, point 3]. The post-market monitoring system itself shall be established and documented in a manner proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks, actively and systematically collecting, documenting and analysing relevant data on performance throughout the system's lifetime [Art. 72(1)] [Art. 72(2)].
citations: Art. 11(1); Annex IV, points 8–9; Annex VII, point 4; Art. 72(3); Annex IV, point 3; Art. 72(1); Art. 72(2)
judge_reason: Core points (EU declaration of conformity; post-market evaluation system and monitoring plan) are correct and well cited; minor extras (Annex IV point 3, Annex VII) and the claim that point 3 relates to 'monitoring' are slightly tangential and not strictly part of the asked items.

question: What will the AI Office do to help companies understand and follow the new AI rules?
answer:
The AI Office will help companies understand and follow the rules by:

*   Providing standardised templates for areas covered by the Regulation, developing and maintaining a single information platform providing easy-to-use information for all operators, organising communication campaigns to raise awareness about obligations, and evaluating and promoting best practices in public procurement procedures in relation to AI systems [Art. 62(3)].
*   Encouraging and facilitating the drawing up of codes of practice at Union level to facilitate the effective implementation of obligations regarding the detection and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content [Art. 50(7)].
*   Encouraging and facilitating the review and adaptation of codes of practice, and assisting in the assessment of available standards [Art. 56(8)].

More generally, the Commission shall develop Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office [Art. 64(1)].
judge_reason: Minor gap: the standardised templates are provided 'as specified by the Board in its request', which the answer omits; otherwise accurate and well-cited.

question: How are the members of the AI scientific panel chosen, and what qualifications do they need?
answer: Members of the scientific panel are selected by the Commission on the basis of up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI necessary for the tasks set out in Article 68(3) [Art. 68(2)]. To be selected, experts must be able to demonstrate that they meet all of the following conditions: (a) having particular expertise and competence and scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI; (b) independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models; and (c) an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively [Art. 68(2)]. The Commission, in consultation with the Board, determines the number of experts on the panel and ensures fair gender and geographical representation [Art. 68(2)]. Once appointed, experts must perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, ensure confidentiality, and neither seek nor take instructions from anyone [Art. 68(4)].

question: Which EU regulation applies to the committee procedure under the AI Act?
answer: Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 applies to the committee procedure under the AI Act [Art. 98(1)]. Specifically, where reference is made to Article 98(2), Article 5 of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 shall apply [Art. 98(2)].

question: What must a national regulator do if an AI system they are checking is also used in other EU countries?
answer:
When a market surveillance authority considers that the non-compliance or use of the AI system is **not restricted to its national territory**, it must **inform the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay** of the results of the evaluation and of the actions it has required the operator (or provider) to take [Art. 79(3)] [Art. 80(3)]. If the AI system is compliant but presents a risk, the Member State must **immediately** inform the Commission and the other Member States, including details on the system’s identification, origin and supply chain, the nature of the risk and the national measures taken [Art. 82(3)].

*(Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.)*
judge_reason: Core answer is correct and cited, but the Art. 82(3) addition is a slight over-extension: that provision depends on a paragraph 1 finding not shown in the excerpts, and 'the Member State' vs the authority is loosely framed.

question: What happens if a serious risk is found while testing an AI system in a regulatory sandbox?
answer: If a significant risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights is identified during testing in an AI regulatory sandbox, it **shall result in an adequate mitigation**. If no effective mitigation is possible, the national competent authority **shall have the power to temporarily or permanently suspend the testing process or the participation in the sandbox**, and must inform the AI Office of that decision [Art. 57(11)].

question: When updating the list of high-risk AI systems, does the Commission look at whether existing EU laws already handle the risks?
answer: Yes. When updating the list of high-risk AI systems in Annex III, the Commission must consider the extent to which existing Union law already addresses the risks. Specifically, when assessing whether to add or modify use-cases under [Art. 7(1)], the Commission shall take into account "the extent to which existing Union law provides for: (i) effective measures of redress in relation to the risks posed by an AI system, with the exclusion of claims for damages; (ii) effective measures to prevent or substantially minimise those risks" [Art. 7(2)(k)].
judge_reason: Minor gap: the answer covers only the adding/modifying route and does not note that Art. 7(3) ties removal to the same Art. 7(2) criteria.

question: Who is allowed to make delegated acts according to Article 97(1)?
answer: The Commission is allowed to make delegated acts [Art. 97(1)].

question: Who is responsible for putting the information into the EU database under Article 71(2)?
answer: The provider, or where applicable, the authorised representative, is responsible for entering the data listed in Sections A and B of Annex VIII into the EU database [Art. 71(2)].

question: What must a company do if their high-risk AI doesn't follow the common specifications?
answer:
If a company's high-risk AI system does not comply with the common specifications, it must duly justify that it has adopted technical solutions meeting the requirements of Section 2 of Chapter III (or, as applicable, the obligations in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter V) to a level at least equivalent thereto [Art. 41(5)].

Additionally, where common specifications exist but the provider has not applied them, the provider shall follow the conformity assessment procedure set out in Annex VII [Art. 43(1)].
judge_reason: Minor gap: the Annex VII point in Art. 43(1) is stated without its limit to Annex III point 1 systems, but the core answer is accurate and well cited.

question: Under Article 82(2), what must a provider do about all the AI systems they have already put on the EU market if they pose a risk?
answer: Under Article 82(2), the provider must ensure that **corrective action is taken in respect of all the AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market**, within the timeline prescribed by the market surveillance authority [Art. 82(2)]. This applies where a compliant high-risk AI system nevertheless presents a risk to health, safety, fundamental rights, or other aspects of public interest [Art. 82(1)].

question: What happens if an approved testing body stops meeting the official requirements?
answer:
The provided excerpts do not use the exact phrase “approved testing body,” but they cover two related situations:

- If a **notified body** no longer meets the requirements or fails its obligations, the notifying authority must investigate, let the body respond, and then **restrict, suspend or withdraw the designation** according to the seriousness of the failure, immediately informing the Commission and other Member States [Art. 36(4)]. After such a measure, the authority must assess the impact on certificates, report within **three months**, require suspension/withdrawal of unduly issued certificates within a reasonable period, and share relevant information with the Commission, Member States and the provider’s national authority [Art. 36(7)]. If the **Commission** finds the notified body does not meet notification requirements, it asks the notifying Member State to take corrective measures, including suspension/withdrawal; if the Member State fails, the Commission may itself suspend, restrict or withdraw the designation by implementing act [Art. 37(4)].

- For **real-world testing**, the market surveillance authority approves the testing and plan; if no answer within **30 days**, tacit approval applies unless national law requires authorisation [Art. 60(4)(b)]. If a serious incident is reported or the authority considers the conditions in Articles 60 and 61 are not met, it may **suspend or terminate the testing** or require modifications [Art. 76(3)].
judge_reason: The core answer on notified bodies (Art. 36(4), 36(7), 37(4)) is accurate and complete, but the answer pads with an unrelated real-world testing paragraph (Art. 60(4)(b), 76(3)) that does not answer the question and the opening hedge is slightly distracting.

question: What can the Commission do after receiving a qualified alert?
answer:
Upon receiving a qualified alert, the Commission may exercise the powers laid down in Section 5 (supervision, investigation, enforcement and monitoring in respect of providers of general-purpose AI models) for the purpose of assessing the matter. This is done through the AI Office and after having informed the Board; the AI Office must then inform the Board of any measure taken according to Articles 91 to 94 [Art. 90(2)].

In addition, the Commission may designate the general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risks, following a qualified alert from the scientific panel under Article 90(1), point (a), on the basis of the criteria set out in Annex XIII [Art. 52(4)].
judge_reason: The 'Section 5 (supervision, investigation, enforcement and monitoring...)' label is not in the retrieved excerpts, though otherwise correct; the Art. 52(4) addition is accurate and grounded.

question: How will the rules for running evaluations and picking outside experts be decided?
answer:
The Commission will adopt implementing acts setting out the detailed arrangements and conditions for the evaluations, including the arrangements for involving independent experts and the procedure for their selection, under the examination procedure referred to in Article 98(2) [Art. 92(6)].

For outside experts, the Commission may appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf, including from the scientific panel, and they must meet the criteria in Article 68(2) [Art. 92(2)]. Those criteria require up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in AI, particular expertise and competence in AI, independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models, and an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively [Art. 68(2)]. The experts must perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, ensure confidentiality, neither seek nor take instructions from anyone, and draw up a publicly available declaration of interests [Art. 68(4)].
judge_reason: Minor: the Art. 68(4) obligations are stated as applying to independent experts for evaluations, though that provision addresses scientific panel members (Art. 92(2) only incorporates Art. 68(2) criteria); otherwise accurate.

question: Do high-risk AI tools need to be supervised by people while they are being used?
answer:
Yes. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so they “can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use” [Art. 14(1)]. Human oversight must aim to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights when the system is used as intended or under reasonably foreseeable misuse [Art. 14(2)], and the measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use [Art. 14(3)].

The deployer must assign oversight to natural persons with “the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support” [Art. 26(2)]. Those overseeing the system must be enabled to understand its capacities and limits and monitor it, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret outputs, decide not to use or to disregard/override/reverse the output, and intervene or stop the system into a safe state [Art. 14(4)]. The instructions for use must also describe the Article 14 human-oversight measures and technical tools facilitating interpretation of outputs [Art. 13(3)(d)]. For certain Annex III point 1(a) systems, no action or decision may be based solely on the system’s identification unless separately verified and confirmed by at least two competent natural persons, except for specified law-enforcement/migration/border-control/asylum uses where EU or national law considers that disproportionate [Art. 14(5)].

question: What rights does an EU agency have before the data protection supervisor fines it?
answer: Before fining a Union institution, body, office or agency, the European Data Protection Supervisor must give it the **opportunity of being heard** on the matter regarding the possible infringement, and must base its decision **only on elements and circumstances on which the parties concerned have been able to comment**; complainants, if any, must be closely associated with the proceedings [Art. 100(4)]. In addition, the **rights of defence** of the parties concerned must be **fully respected**, and they are entitled to **access to the EDPS’s file**, subject to the legitimate interest of individuals or undertakings in protecting their personal data or business secrets [Art. 100(5)]. When deciding whether to impose a fine and its amount, the EDPS must also take into account all relevant circumstances, including the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, the degree of responsibility and cooperation, mitigation of damage, previous infringements, how the infringement became known, and the agency’s annual budget [Art. 100(1)].

question: Who is responsible for adding the notified body's ID number next to the CE mark, and where else does it need to appear?
answer: The notified body’s identification number shall be affixed by the body itself or, under its instructions, by the provider or by the provider’s authorised representative [Art. 48(4)]. It shall also be indicated in any promotional material which mentions that the high-risk AI system fulfils the requirements for CE marking [Art. 48(4)].

question: What should a company do if they realize their high-risk AI product doesn't meet the rules after releasing it?
answer:
If a provider considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation, it must **immediately take the necessary corrective actions** to bring that system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it, as appropriate, and shall inform the distributors, and where applicable the deployers, the authorised representative and importers accordingly [Art. 20(1)].

Where the high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it shall **immediately investigate the causes**, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the certificate, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken [Art. 20(2)].

This is not legal advice.

question: When does a company that makes a product count as the provider of a high-risk AI safety component inside it?
answer:
A product manufacturer is considered the provider of a high-risk AI safety component inside its product when that AI system meets the high-risk conditions in [Art. 6(1)]—i.e., it is intended as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment (“safety component” is defined in [Art. 3(14)])—and either:

- the high-risk AI system is placed on the market together with the product under the name or trademark of the product manufacturer; or
- the high-risk AI system is put into service under the name or trademark of the product manufacturer after the product has been placed on the market [Art. 25(3)].
judge_reason: Content is accurate, but it omits that Art. 25(3) applies to Annex I Section A legislation and that the manufacturer then bears Art. 16 provider obligations, and it blurs classification (Art. 6(1)) with the manufacturer-as-provider rule.

question: Do open-source AI models get any exemptions from the rules for general-purpose AI?
answer:
Yes. Open-source general-purpose AI (GPAI) models benefit from specific exemptions, but only under strict conditions and with key limits.

**Exemptions for GPAI model obligations:** The obligations in Article 53(1)(a) and (b) do not apply to providers of GPAI models released under a free and open-source licence that allows access, usage, modification and distribution, provided the model’s parameters—including weights, architecture information and usage information—are made publicly available [Art. 53(2)]. The same exemption applies to the obligation to appoint an authorised representative [Art. 54(6)].

**Systemic risk carve-out:** These exemptions do not apply to GPAI models that present systemic risks [Art. 53(2)], [Art. 54(6)]. Recital 104 confirms that an open-source licence is not a sufficient reason to exclude compliance when the model presents a systemic risk [Recital 104].

**Scope exclusion:** The Regulation does not apply at all to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or fall under Article 5 (prohibited practices) or Article 50 [Art. 2(12)].

**Limits on the exemption:** Even when the transparency-related exceptions apply, they do not cover the obligation to produce a summary of the training content or to put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including respecting reservations of rights under Directive (EU) 2019/790 [Recital 104]. Furthermore, AI components provided against a price or otherwise monetised do not benefit from the open-source exceptions [Recital 103].

**Definition:** A licence qualifies as free and open-source for GPAI models only if it allows users to freely access, use, modify and redistribute the model or modified versions, and the parameters (weights, architecture, usage information) are publicly available [Recital 102].
citations: Art. 53(2); Art. 54(6); Recital 104; Art. 2(12); Recital 103; Recital 102
judge_reason: Accurate and well-grounded; minor imprecision in describing Art. 54(6) as 'the obligation to appoint an authorised representative' (not explicit in excerpt) and tying the monetisation limit generally rather than specifically.

question: Can a notified body hire another company or use a subsidiary to do part of an AI assessment, and what must they do if they do?
answer:
Yes. A notified body may subcontract specific conformity-assessment tasks or use a subsidiary, but only with the provider’s agreement, and it must make a list of its subsidiaries publicly available [Art. 33(3)].

The requirements are:
- The notified body must ensure the subcontractor or subsidiary meets the requirements laid down in Article 31 and must inform the notifying authority accordingly [Art. 33(1)].
- The notified body takes full responsibility for tasks performed by any subcontractor or subsidiary [Art. 33(2)].
- Documents on the subcontractor’s/subsidiary’s qualifications and the work performed must be kept available to the notifying authority for five years from the termination date of the subcontracting [Art. 33(4)].

question: If a company qualifies for a special innovation exemption, does it still have to follow the rest of the AI Act's rules?
answer:
No. The excerpts show that innovation support measures provide only narrow relief, not a general exemption from the rest of the Act’s rules.

- Liability is not waived: providers in sandboxes “shall remain liable under applicable Union and national liability law for any damage inflicted on third parties” [Art. 57(12)].
- Only administrative fines may be waived, and only under strict conditions: no fines are imposed “provided that the prospective providers observe the specific plan and the terms and conditions for their participation and follow in good faith the guidance given by the national competent authority” [Art. 57(12)].
- Supervisory and corrective powers remain fully in place: sandboxes “shall not affect the supervisory or corrective powers of the competent authorities,” and authorities may suspend testing if significant risks are not adequately mitigated [Art. 57(11)].
- Simplified compliance still requires full protection: microenterprises may use a simplified quality management system, but only “without affecting the level of protection or the need for compliance with the requirements in respect of high-risk AI systems” [Art. 63(1)].
judge_reason: The answer reaches the right conclusion and its claims are grounded and accurately cited, but it omits the explicit provision that the microenterprise simplification does not exempt operators from other obligations, i.e. Art. 63(2), and its 'narrow relief' framing is only inferred from the excerpts.

question: How should banks or other financial companies store the automatic logs from their high-risk AI?
answer: Financial institutions subject to requirements under Union financial services law must store the automatically generated logs as part of the documentation kept under the relevant financial services law, both when acting as providers [Art. 19(2)] and as deployers [Art. 26(6)]. While the general rule requires keeping such logs for a period of at least six months unless provided otherwise in applicable law [Art. 19(1)] [Art. 26(6)], for financial institutions this storage is integrated into the documentation maintained pursuant to the relevant Union financial service law [Art. 19(2)] [Art. 26(6)].

question: Can a company challenge a fine or penalty given under the AI Act?
answer: Yes. For fines imposed by the Commission on providers of general-purpose AI models under Article 101, the Court of Justice of the European Union has “unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine” and “may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed” [Art. 101(5)]. In addition, before adopting such a decision, the Commission must give the provider “an opportunity to be heard” [Art. 101(2)]. The provided excerpts do not address challenge mechanisms for fines under other provisions, such as Articles 99 or 100.
judge_reason: Accurate on Art. 101(5) and 101(2), but misses the gold provision Art. 99(10) (effective judicial remedies and due process for national fines) and wrongly implies the Act does not address challenges for Article 99 fines.

question: What rules do authorities have to follow when they collect and handle data about AI systems?
answer:
Authorities must request only data that is "strictly necessary" for assessing the risk posed by AI systems and exercising their powers, implement "adequate and effective cybersecurity measures" to protect security and confidentiality, and "delete the data collected as soon as it is no longer needed" [Art. 78(2)].

Information and documentation obtained by competent authorities and market surveillance authorities must be handled in accordance with confidentiality obligations that protect intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets, effective implementation of the Regulation, public and national security interests, proceedings, and classified information [Art. 78(1)], [Art. 21(3)], [Art. 74(14)].

Information exchanged on a confidential basis between national competent authorities or with the Commission may not be disclosed without prior consultation of the originating authority (and the deployer for certain Annex III systems used by law enforcement, border control, immigration or asylum authorities), and such exchanges must not cover sensitive operational data of those authorities [Art. 78(3)].

The EU database for high-risk AI systems may contain personal data only "in so far as necessary," limited to the names and contact details of natural persons responsible for registering the system [Art. 71(5)].
judge_reason: Core rule from Art. 78(2) is accurate and complete; minor imprecision: Art. 78(3) non-disclosure is conditioned on public/national security jeopardy, and Art. 71(5) personal data is described as 'limited to' names/contact details whereas the text says 'shall include'.

question: Do I need to include every single detail in the technical paperwork for my AI system?
answer: No. The technical documentation must contain "at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV" [Art. 11(1)], but Annex IV only requires information "as applicable to the relevant AI system" [Annex IV]. Certain detailed information—such as monitoring, functioning, control, capabilities, limitations, and foreseeable unintended outcomes—is required only where relevant to the system's intended purpose [Annex IV, point 3]. Additionally, SMEs, including start-ups, may provide these elements "in a simplified manner" using a Commission-established form [Art. 11(1)].
citations: Art. 11(1); Annex IV; Annex IV, point 3
judge_reason: Mostly correct, but the claim that Annex IV point 3 information is required 'only where relevant' overstates the text, which only qualifies 'specifications on input data' with 'as appropriate'; also the answer does not stress that all Annex IV elements apply insofar as applicable and that the documentation must be a minimum and kept up to date.

question: If my AI system follows official EU standards, does that mean it automatically meets the AI Act's rules?
answer:
No. Following official EU standards does not mean your AI system automatically meets the AI Act’s rules; it creates a **presumption of conformity**, and only to the extent the standards actually cover the relevant requirements.

Key conditions from the excerpts:

*   High-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models in conformity with harmonised standards (references published in the Official Journal) “shall be presumed to be in conformity” with the Chapter III requirements or Chapter V obligations **“to the extent that those standards cover those requirements or obligations”** [Art. 40(1)].
*   The same applies to common specifications: conformity “shall be presumed” only **“to the extent those common specifications cover those requirements or those obligations”** [Art. 41(3)].
*   If harmonised standards do not exist, are not fully applied, or are applied only in part, the provider must instead follow the conformity assessment procedure in Annex VII [Art. 43(1)].

This is not legal advice.
judge_reason: Minor issue: Art. 43(1) Annex VII fallback is stated for point 1 Annex III systems, but the answer presents it generally.

question: What types of infrastructure are covered as high-risk AI under Annex III point 2?
answer:
Under Annex III, point 2, high-risk AI systems include those intended to be used as **safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or in the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity** [Annex III, point 2].

Recital 55 clarifies that this covers critical digital infrastructure as listed in Directive (EU) 2022/2557, road traffic, and the supply of water, gas, heating and electricity, because their failure or malfunctioning may put the life and health of persons at large scale at risk [Recital 55].

question: Can a notifying authority also offer paid consulting services or do the same work as a testing body?
answer:
No. Notifying authorities are explicitly prohibited from both activities. [Art. 28(5)]

Under the AI Act, notifying authorities "shall offer or provide neither any activities that conformity assessment bodies perform, nor any consultancy services on a commercial or competitive basis" [Art. 28(5)]. They must also be organised and operated so that "no conflict of interest arises with conformity assessment bodies" and their objectivity and impartiality are safeguarded [Art. 28(3)].

question: How and where do I need to put the CE mark on a high-risk AI product?
answer:
According to the EU AI Act, you must affix the CE marking **visibly, legibly and indelibly** on the high-risk AI system itself [Art. 48(3)]. If that is not possible or not warranted due to the nature of the system, you must affix it to the **packaging or accompanying documentation** instead [Art. 48(3)].

For high-risk AI systems **provided digitally**, you must use a **digital CE marking** that can easily be accessed via the interface from which the system is accessed, or via an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means [Art. 48(2)].

Where applicable, the CE marking must be followed by the **identification number of the notified body** responsible for the conformity assessment; this number is affixed by the body itself or under its instructions, and must also appear in any promotional material mentioning CE conformity [Art. 48(4)].

As a provider, you are obligated to affix the CE marking to the system (or its packaging/documentation where not possible) to indicate conformity [Art. 16(h)]. The CE marking indicates that the system conforms with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 and other applicable Union harmonisation legislation [Art. 3(24)].
judge_reason: Minor: states the digital marking 'must' be used for digital systems, while Art. 48(2) conditions it on easy accessibility, and omits the Art. 48(5) point on other Union law.

question: What can a fundamental rights body do if the paperwork isn't enough to tell whether a high-risk AI broke the law?
answer: If the technical documentation is insufficient to ascertain whether a high-risk AI system has infringed obligations protecting fundamental rights, the fundamental rights body may make a **reasoned request to the market surveillance authority to organise testing of the high-risk AI system through technical means**; the market surveillance authority must organise this testing with the close involvement of the requesting body within a reasonable time [Art. 77(3)]. This power builds on the body's general right to request and access any documentation created or maintained under the Regulation when necessary for fulfilling its mandate [Art. 77(1)].

question: When is a general-purpose AI considered to have systemic risk?
answer:
A general-purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk when it meets any of the conditions in Article 51(1): either it has “high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks” [Art. 51(1)], or the Commission decides—ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel—that it has “capabilities or an impact equivalent to those” based on the criteria in Annex XIII [Art. 51(1)].

Additionally, a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations [Art. 51(2)]. If a provider’s arguments that the model does not present systemic risks are “not sufficiently substantiated” and the provider cannot demonstrate the absence of such risks, the model shall be considered to have systemic risk [Art. 52(3)]. The Commission may also designate a model as presenting systemic risks ex officio or following a qualified alert, on the basis of Annex XIII criteria [Art. 52(4)].

“Systemic risk” itself is defined as a risk specific to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models that has a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or society as a whole, that can be propagated at scale across the value chain [Art. 3(65)].

question: What information do authorities have to share when they report a risky or rule-breaking AI system?
answer:
When authorities report a risky or rule-breaking AI system, they must share the following information:

**For compliant AI systems that present a risk**, Member States must immediately inform the Commission and other Member States, including "all available details, in particular the data necessary for the identification of the AI system concerned, the origin and the supply chain of the AI system, the nature of the risk involved and the nature and duration of the national measures taken" [Art. 82(3)].

**For non-compliant AI systems**, market surveillance authorities must inform the Commission and other Member States of "any measures adopted and of any additional information at their disposal relating to the non-compliance of the AI system concerned", and, if they disagree with a notified national measure, "of their objections" [Art. 79(7)].

**When the use is not restricted to national territory**, authorities must share "the results of the evaluation and of the actions which it has required the provider to take" [Art. 80(3)].

**Regarding prohibited practices and competition**, authorities must annually report to the Commission "any information identified... that may be of potential interest for the application of Union law on competition rules", as well as information "about the use of prohibited practices... and about the measures taken" [Art. 74(2)]. For real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces, they must submit annual reports including "the number of the decisions taken by competent judicial authorities... and their result" [Art. 5(6)].

**For prudential supervision**, national authorities must report to the European Central Bank "any information identified... that may be of potential interest for the prudential supervisory tasks of the European Central Bank" [Art. 74(7)].
judge_reason: The answer omits the gold Art. 79(6) content (identification of the system, origin/supply chain, nature of non-compliance and risk, measures, operator arguments, and the Art. 5/Chapter III/standards/Art. 50 breakdown), though that provision was not retrieved; instead it relies on Art. 79(7), which covers only other authorities' follow-up information, and Art. 82(3), which is accurate for risk findings.

question: Are there any situations where the right to an explanation for an AI decision doesn't apply?
answer: Yes. The right to an explanation does not apply where exceptions or restrictions to that obligation follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law [Art. 86(2)]. It also applies only to the extent that the right is not already otherwise provided for under Union law [Art. 86(3)]. These limits are reflected in the recitals as well [Recital 171].

question: What needs to be considered when making sure a high-risk AI system meets the rules in Article 8(1)?
answer: When ensuring a high-risk AI system complies with the requirements in Article 8(1), the following must be taken into account: the system's **intended purpose**, the **generally acknowledged state of the art on AI and AI-related technologies**, and the **risk management system referred to in Article 9** [Art. 8(1)].

question: What factors determine what goes into the technical documentation for a general-purpose AI model?
answer:
The content of the technical documentation for a general-purpose AI model is determined by the **size and risk profile of the model**, and by whether the model poses **systemic risk**. [Annex XI, Section 1] [Annex XI, Section 2, points 1–3]

Specifically:

*   All providers must include information "as appropriate to the size and risk profile of the model," including a general description (tasks, acceptable use policies, date of release, architecture and number of parameters, modality and format of inputs/outputs, and the licence) and a detailed description of development elements (technical means for integration, design specifications and training process, data used, computational resources, and energy consumption). [Annex XI, Section 1] [Annex XI, Section 1, point 1] [Annex XI, Section 1, point 2]
*   Providers of models **with systemic risk** must additionally provide a detailed description of evaluation strategies and results, measures for adversarial testing and model adaptations, and the system architecture. [Annex XI, Section 2, points 1–3]

The documentation also differs based on its **recipient**: documentation for the AI Office and national competent authorities must contain the elements in Annex XI, while information provided to downstream providers integrating the model must contain the elements in Annex XII. [Art. 53(1)]
citations: Annex XI, Section 1; Annex XI, Section 2, points 1–3; Annex XI, Section 1, point 1; Annex XI, Section 1, point 2; Art. 53(1)
judge_reason: Answer is accurate and well-cited; the main factor (size and risk profile) is stated, though the 'systemic risk' framing is slightly beyond the gold text and the Annex XII recipient point is tangential but supported.

question: How can companies making general-purpose AI prove they follow the rules?
answer:
Providers of general-purpose AI models can demonstrate compliance with their obligations through three routes:

*   **Codes of practice:** They may rely on codes of practice within the meaning of Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with the obligations set out in Article 53(1) (or Article 55(1) for models with systemic risk), until a harmonised standard is published [Art. 53(4)], [Art. 55(2)]. These codes are intended as a central compliance tool and may be approved by the Commission to have general validity within the Union [Recital 117].

*   **European harmonised standards:** Compliance with these standards grants providers a presumption of conformity to the extent that the standards cover the relevant obligations [Art. 53(4)], [Art. 55(2)], [Recital 117].

*   **Alternative adequate means:** Providers who do not adhere to an approved code of practice or do not comply with a European harmonised standard must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission [Art. 53(4)], [Art. 55(2)]. This option is also available if codes or standards are not available or if the provider chooses not to rely on them [Recital 117].

The underlying obligations include drawing up and maintaining technical documentation, providing information to downstream AI system providers, implementing a copyright compliance policy, and publishing a summary of training content [Art. 53(1)].

question: Does the EU look at power imbalances or vulnerability when deciding if an AI system is high-risk?
answer: Yes. When assessing whether to amend Annex III (the list of high-risk AI systems), the Commission must consider the extent of any imbalance of power or the vulnerable position of persons potentially harmed, including factors such as status, authority, knowledge, economic or social circumstances, or age [Art. 7(2)(h)]. It must also consider whether affected persons are dependent on the AI system’s outcome and cannot reasonably opt out [Art. 7(2)(g)], and whether the harm can disproportionately affect a particular group [Art. 7(2)(f)]. Additionally, once a system is classified as high-risk, providers must consider whether it is likely to adversely impact persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups when implementing the risk management system [Art. 9(9)].

question: Do companies making high-risk AI have to keep records of their documents?
answer: Yes. Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep specific documentation at the disposal of national competent authorities for **10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service**, including: the technical documentation, the quality management system documentation, documentation on changes approved by notified bodies (where applicable), decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies (where applicable), and the EU declaration of conformity [Art. 18(1)]. The quality management system itself must include systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information [Art. 17(1)(k)]. Separately, the provider must keep the EU declaration of conformity for the same 10-year period [Art. 47(1)], and the high-risk AI system itself must technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over its lifetime [Art. 12(1)].

question: What does a company have to do before launching an AI system they believe isn't high-risk?
answer: A company that considers its AI system not high-risk must, before placing it on the market or putting it into service: (1) document its assessment that the system is not high-risk [Art. 6(4)]; and (2) register itself and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 [Art. 49(2)], [Art. 6(4)]. Upon request of national competent authorities, the provider must also provide the documentation of that assessment [Art. 6(4)].

question: If a regulator objects to real-world AI testing or makes a decision about it, what information do they have to give the provider?
answer: The regulator must indicate **the grounds** for the decision or objection and **how the provider or prospective provider can challenge** it [Art. 76(4)].

question: How are the rules set for the scientific panel to send out warnings or ask the AI Office for help?
answer:
The rules are set out in an implementing act, which must include provisions on the **conditions, procedures and detailed arrangements** for the scientific panel and its members **to issue alerts** and **to request the assistance of the AI Office** for the performance of the panel’s tasks [Art. 68(5)].

As regards the alerts themselves, the scientific panel may provide a **qualified alert** to the AI Office where it has reason to suspect that a general-purpose AI model poses a concrete identifiable risk at Union level or meets the conditions referred to in Article 51 [Art. 90(1)]. Such a qualified alert must be **duly reasoned** and indicate at least the point of contact of the provider, a description of the relevant facts and reasons, and any other relevant information the panel considers appropriate [Art. 90(3)].

question: If my AI model is classified as having systemic risk, how soon can I ask the Commission to review that decision?
answer:
You may request reassessment at the earliest **six months after the designation decision** [Art. 52(5)]. The request must be reasoned and contain "objective, detailed and new reasons that have arisen since the designation decision" [Art. 52(5)]. If the Commission decides to maintain the designation following reassessment, you may request reassessment again at the earliest six months after that decision [Art. 52(5)].

This is not legal advice.

question: Do national authorities get flexibility when setting up AI regulatory sandboxes?
answer:
Yes. The implementing acts must ensure that the detailed arrangements and conditions for AI regulatory sandboxes support, “to the best extent possible, flexibility for national competent authorities to establish and operate their AI regulatory sandboxes” [Art. 58(2)(c)].

Flexibility is also reflected in how sandboxes may be established: at national level, jointly with other Member States, or by participating in an existing sandbox where that provides equivalent national coverage [Art. 57(1)], and additional sandboxes may be established at regional or local level or jointly with other Member States [Art. 57(2)].

question: Who sets the detailed rules and safeguards for fining companies that make general-purpose AI?
answer: The Commission sets them: it “shall adopt implementing acts containing detailed arrangements and procedural safeguards” for fining proceedings against providers of general-purpose AI models, adopted under the examination procedure in Article 98(2) [Art. 101(6)].

question: Who can fine EU agencies if they break the AI rules, and what factors determine the amount?
answer:
The **European Data Protection Supervisor** may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the scope of the Regulation [Art. 100(1)].

When deciding whether to impose a fine and its amount, it must consider all relevant circumstances and give due regard to: (a) the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, the purpose of the AI system, the number of affected persons and the level of damage; (b) the degree of responsibility, taking into account technical and organisational measures; (c) any action taken to mitigate damage to affected persons; (d) the degree of cooperation with the European Data Protection Supervisor to remedy the infringement and mitigate adverse effects, including compliance with previously ordered measures; (e) any similar previous infringements; (f) how the infringement became known, in particular whether and to what extent the institution notified it; and (g) the annual budget of the institution, body, office or agency [Art. 100(1)].

The maximum fines are EUR 1 500 000 for non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibitions [Art. 100(2)] and EUR 750 000 for other non-compliance [Art. 100(3)].

question: After finishing a fundamental rights assessment for a high-risk AI system, who do I have to report the results to?
answer: You must notify the **market surveillance authority** of the results, submitting the filled-out template as part of the notification [Art. 27(3)]. In the case referred to in Article 46(1), you may be exempt from that obligation to notify [Art. 27(3)].

question: What responsibility does a company take on when it issues a conformity declaration for a high-risk AI system, and must it keep the document current?
answer:
When a provider draws up the EU declaration of conformity, it **assumes responsibility for compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2** [Art. 47(4)].

Yes, the provider **must keep the EU declaration of conformity up-to-date as appropriate** [Art. 47(4)]. In addition, the provider must keep the declaration at the disposal of national competent authorities for **10 years** after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service [Art. 47(1)].

question: Do I need to set up a risk management process for high-risk AI?
answer:
Yes. If you are a provider of a high-risk AI system, you must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system [Art. 9(1)]. This system must also be included in your quality management system [Art. 17(1)(g)], which you are required to put in place [Art. 16].

The risk management system must be a continuous, iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of the high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It must comprise: (a) identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights when used in accordance with its intended purpose; (b) estimation and evaluation of risks that may emerge under intended use and conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse; (c) evaluation of other risks possibly arising from post-market monitoring data; and (d) adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures to address the risks identified [Art. 9(2)].

This is not legal advice.
judge_reason: Answer is accurate and well-cited; minor gap: it doesn't mention Art. 9(2)(d) risks are those from point (a) only, and frames the duty as provider-specific when Art. 9(1) itself doesn't name an actor.
